title: browser-use/browser-use 0.13.14 — 0.13.14: Python agent and integration updates
body:
This release keeps the Python agent and its existing models. The Pi migration remains separate.

Changes since the last PyPI release:
- Add OpenAI browser tools and the shared Bash helper.
- Improve bounded page observations, form state, file access, and browser recovery.
- Fix temporary empty Cloud tab URLs.
- Keep screenshots, crops, and clicks aligned on scaled displays.
- Clean up failed browser reconnect initialization.
- Improve missing-key errors for Cloud browsers.
- Support Browser Use Cloud SDK V4 imports.
- Update aiohttp from 3.14.3 to 3.14.5.
- Refresh Cloud guidance and saved-task replay examples.

Validation:
- GitHub checks pass on the exact release source.
- Pre-commit passes for the version change.
- The wheel and source package build successfully.
- Package metadata and all five CLI entries pass validation.
- All 171 packaged Python files match the existing Python runtime.
- The installed wheel runs `browser-use --help`.

Install with `uv add browser-use==0.13.14` or `pip install browser-use==0.13.14`.

The protected publishing workflow requires another release reviewer. PyPI publication follows that approval.

title: agno-agi/agno v3.1.12 — v3.1.12
body:
# Changelog

## New Features:

- **Native Approvals for Harness Agents**: Claude's and Codex's own permission requests now reach the AgentOS approval UI. When the agent has a database, including one AgentOS supplies, a native request persists a PAUSED run that shows up in the existing chat and Approvals views, and Resolve plus Continue Run delivers the decision back to the same native execution without replaying the prompt. The harness's own policy decides when to ask — Claude keeps its `permission_mode` and explicit permission callbacks, Codex supports `approval_policy="on-request" | "untrusted" | "never"` alongside its existing SDK `auto_review` and `deny_all` modes — so there is no separate Agno setting to turn on. Decisions are validated against the exact action requested, with sync and async continuation, cancellation, expiry and storage-failure handling, and sandboxed agents keep this across Docker and AgentCore: capability negotiation, a decision RPC, fenced persistence, reattachment after an API-worker loss, separate approval-wait and execution budgets, and no replay after process loss. Note that a `CodexAgent` with no approval settings now runs under the native `on-request` policy, so a request that previously went nowhere pauses the run instead; `hitl_timeout` (default 900s) bounds how long it waits. See `cookbook/frameworks/human_in_the_loop/`.
- **Initially Disabled Company Routines**: `Routine(enabled=False)` lets a template ship an inactive Routine that a user turns on later from the UI, with `True` still the default. Disabled Routines are created atomically, stay linked to their Product and visible in listings, are skipped by the scheduler, and keep the user's saved choice across restarts. The flag is honored in Python and YAML bootstrap, the setup and creation APIs, the sync and async Company Manager, and the Company tools. Duplicate create requests still return `409` and cannot enable an existing Routine, and the existing pause/resume endpoints enable it without recreating it. See `cookbook/05_agent_os/30_company/11_disabled_routine.py`.
- **Headline Numbers on Charts**: `ChartTools.create_chart()` takes an optional preformatted `value` — a total or latest value such as `"$22.3K"` or `"94%"` — emitted as `"value"` in the chart block and rendered by Agno OS beside the chart title. The docstring tells the model to leave it out when no single number summarizes the chart, so averages and rates are not summed.

## Improvements:

- **Company Routine Sorting**: `GET /company/routines` now also sorts by `next_run_at`, `schedule_type` and `enabled`, so Agno OS can sort its routines table by Next run at, Schedule and Active. Paused and on-demand Routines have no upcoming run, so they come last in either direction, and Routines with the same value keep their creation order.
- **Cookbooks**: Added an `ApifyTools` job search example that caps the Actor's item count with a tool hook and trims each dataset item to title, company, loc

title: agno-agi/agno v3.1.11 — v3.1.11
body:
# Changelog

## New Features:

- **Harness Agents in Teams and Workflows**: `ClaudeAgent` and `CodexAgent` can now be members of an Agno `Team` and steps of a `Workflow`, including inside `Parallel`, `Loop`, `Condition` and `Router`. The team leader delegates to them with `delegate_task_to_member` like any other member, each harness runs with its own model, tools and workspace, keeps its own conversation across turns of the same session, and the team or workflow collects its runs as usual. A harness agent with `sandbox=` runs each turn in its own container as a member or step, and AgentOS lists harness members on the team page. See `cookbook/frameworks/harness_teams/` and `cookbook/frameworks/harness_workflows/`.
- **Session Search**: Added `GET /sessions/filter-schema` and `POST /sessions/search` with nested AND/OR/NOT filters on session name, session/user/component IDs, session type and created/updated timestamps, matching the Traces API. Predicates are applied before counting and pagination in PostgreSQL and SQLite, with a batched fallback for other adapters. Sync and async client methods are included.
- **Company Tasks**: `POST /company/tasks` accepts `status`, so Tasks can be created in Backlog, Ready or Cancelled. Tasks can move between any stages, Done and Cancelled Tasks can reopen, and title and brief can be edited at any stage. In progress still starts only with a run, and moving out of it while that run is executing or paused is refused.
- **Company Routines**: Added `POST /company/routines/{id}/cancel`, `/archive`, `/restore` and admin-only `DELETE /company/routines/{id}`. `GET /company/routines` takes `sort_by` and `sort_order`. Pause and resume on an on-demand Routine return `409`, and scheduler runs no longer move `updated_at`.

## Improvements:

- **Cookbooks**: Added a customer feedback workflow for the AgentOS UI, where Company Manager reads Markdown feedback, proposes evidence-backed Projects and Backlog Tasks, and leaves acceptance to a human.
- **README**: Aligned the README with the docs introduction and the self-improving agent platform positioning.

## Bug Fixes:

- **ReaderFactory**: `create_reader()` now returns a fresh reader configured with the per-call options instead of a cached singleton, so `chunk_size` and other overrides are respected and mutations no longer leak across `Knowledge` instances.
- **Workflow Step Content**: `StepOutput.to_dict()` keeps ints, floats, bools and strs as themselves instead of stringifying them, so a step that returned `0` or `False` no longer comes back as `"0"` or `"False"` after a HITL resume, a session reload, or through the AgentOS workflow API.
- **HuggingFace**: `default_headers` is mapped to the SDK's `headers`, `store` is sent in `extra_body`, and `max_retries` and `default_query` are deprecated and ignored instead of raising `TypeError`. An agent with no tools no longer sends `tools=[]`, which made non-streaming runs return `None` content.

title: modelcontextprotocol/servers v2.2.0 — v2.2.0
body:
## Security: Node.js runtime and CA certificate updates (October 2026)

On October 20, 2026, eMudhra disclosed that the private keys for eight of its intermediate CA certificates could be recovered from the public certificates. On October 21, Node.js shipped [security releases](https://nodejs.org/en/blog/vulnerability/october-2026-security-releases) that update its bundled CA certificates for the compromise and fix several unrelated high-severity runtime CVEs. On October 23, Python's `certifi` 2026.10.23 removed the eMudhra roots `emSign Root CA - C1` and `emSign ECC Root CA - C3`.

**How these servers stand**

- **The TypeScript servers rely on the Node.js runtime for certificate checks.** They ship no CA certificates of their own. Only `server-everything` makes outbound HTTPS requests (`gzip-file-as-resource`), and the Node.js it runs on verifies them. `server-filesystem`, `server-memory` and `server-sequential-thinking` make no network connections.
- **`mcp-server-fetch` verifies HTTPS against the `certifi` bundle**, through `httpx`. Installing from PyPI (`uvx mcp-server-fetch`, `pip install mcp-server-fetch`) resolves the current `certifi`, 2026.10.23 or later. The repository's `fetch` Dockerfile installs from its lockfile, which this release moves to `certifi` 2026.10.23 (#5341).
- **`mcp-server-git` and `mcp-server-time` make no network connections.**

**If you run a TypeScript server from npm (`npx` or a global install)**

title: In-Model Context Compression with Agentic Soft Tokens for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
body: Long-horizon LLM agents play an important role in solving complex and sustained tasks, with ever-growing interaction contexts. However, these accumulated contexts will raise substantial computational cost and obscure key decision-relevant evidence. Existing methods typically train external compressors or context-management agents to rewrite context as shorter hard-token sequences, but such external selection may not align with the LLM's evolving representation and is necessarily lossy. In this paper, we introduce Agentic Soft-Token Compression (ASTC), a training-free compression method using soft tokens within LLM agent for long-horizon tasks. Specifically, ASTC uses the model's native recurrent dynamics to determine the already absorbed information, leveraging the commonly-used hybrid Gated Delta Network (GDN)-attention. It then carries this information forward as agentic soft tokens while retaining exact values as hard tokens. The resulting compact sequence reduces later-layer computation and yields reusable KV caches, extending the savings across the agent's trajectory. Extensive experiments on long-horizon tasks show that ASTC matches or exceeds the uncompressed agent's accuracy with up to 50.68% fewer end-to-end Attention Pairs, while trained compressors require 15.4 to 103.7 times more Attention Pairs per successful task. These findings highlight agentic soft tokens as a model-native way to carry absorbed context forward as the task representation evolves.

title: Don't Lose the Thread: Empowering Long-Horizon LLM Agents with Cognitive Resource Self-Allocation
body: Agents powered by large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable progress in solving complex reasoning tasks. However, LLM agents often falter on long-horizon tasks due to cognitive overload, as their working memory becomes cluttered with expanding and irrelevant information, which dilutes their attention and hinders effective planning and reasoning. To mitigate this challenge, we introduce Cognitive Resource Self-Allocation (CORAL), a novel reasoning paradigm that empowers agents to proactively optimize their context. Implemented as an agent-callable working memory management toolset, CORAL allows an agent to checkpoint its task progress and verified facts, and adaptively initiate a new problem-solving episode by resetting cluttered context while preserving only the checkpointed information, enabling it to resume reasoning from a clean state. We further enhance the agent's checkpointing capabilities using a Multi-episode Agentic Reinforced Policy Optimization algorithm. On the GAIA benchmark, CORAL with an 8B model achieves 42.8% average accuracy, with particularly strong gains on the most challenging long-horizon tasks (Level 2 and Level 3). Crucially, these gains come at a substantially lower inference cost: CORAL consumes 6-7$\times$ fewer input tokens than a ReAct agent. It also generalizes to multi-hop Knowledge QA benchmarks and to the considerably harder BrowseComp, where it improves a strong proprietary agent by 8.0 points.

title: Verify--Backtrack Loop: Structured Precondition Recovery for Long-Horizon Language Agents
body: Language agents increasingly tackle long-horizon tasks in interactive environments, where actions often depend on latent preconditions. The core difficulty is not trajectory length but recovery: when a prerequisite is missing or an earlier decomposition fails, trying another plausible action rarely helps. ReAct and later reflection or adaptive-planning methods support local correction, but express recovery as free-form text, with no explicit control state linking the terminal goal, the active goal, and the failure source. We introduce the Verify--Backtrack Loop (VBL), a training-free extension of ReAct that turns precondition discovery and failure diagnosis into structured planning-state updates. VBL maintains the task decomposition as a bounded goal stack and, on goal activation, execution failure, or material state change, jointly verifies two horizons---whether the active goal contributes to the terminal goal and whether it is feasible in the current state. These dual-horizon judgments, combined with typed failure attribution, trigger explicit operations---Push, Pop, retry, or BacktrackTo the parent. We evaluate VBL with Qwen3.5-9B, GPT-4o, and DeepSeek-V3.2 on AppWorld, ALFWorld, and ScienceWorld. VBL improves over ReAct and reflection-based control on every backbone--benchmark pair. On the challenging AppWorld setting, it improves task success by up to 22.07 percentage points over ReAct. Ablations show that removing either verification or diagnosis degrades performance, in several settings below ReAct, confirming that the two mechanisms are complementary. These results show that reliable long-horizon interaction benefits from revising the planning state, not merely the next action.

title: VeriCUA: Verification as Agentic Exploration for Computer-Using Agents
body: Building and scaling computer-using agents (CUAs) across desktop, mobile, and web environments requires reliable task-completion verification for data curation, evaluation, and reinforcement learning. Typical automated approaches prompt vision-language models (VLMs) to judge trajectories or generate programs to inspect application state. However, both rely on partial views of complex digital environments. VLM judges are restricted to supplied observations, while generated programs depend on accessible state. These views can omit decisive evidence or leave completion judgments unsupported. Tailoring separate verifiers to different platforms and access settings adds further engineering cost. We present VeriCUA, a platform-agnostic framework for verification through agentic exploration. It treats verification as dynamic evidence gathering and assessment within a shared procedure for online and offline settings across platforms and observation modalities. After inspecting the available context to construct a task rubric, the verifier selects GUI or code checks for unresolved requirements and combines their findings under explicit evidence rules. Experiments show improved agreement with reference labels over the compared baselines across these settings, with the largest offline gains on hard cases and stronger rejection of false completion claims online. Further analyses connect these gains to complementary evidence and test-time exploration.

title: TradeWar: A Benchmark for Execution-Grounded Trade Negotiation with Adaptive LLM Agents
body: Multi-turn negotiation remains a challenging problem for large language model (LLM) agents. While LLMs can conduct natural-language dialogue, existing benchmarks predominantly assess only agreement rates, overlooking whether negotiated commitments actually create value once executed. To address this gap, we introduce TradeWar, a multi-country simulation benchmark that translates negotiation dialogues into concrete tariff and trade-share policies, enforces capacity and network constraints during settlement, and evaluates outcomes via an Economic Health Index (EHI). To solve this execution-grounded task, we propose TACTIC (Trade-aware Adaptive Consolidation and Theory-of-mind for International Commerce), an agent that iteratively refines its negotiation strategy across episodes-without updating base LLM weights-by leveraging prior experience, opponent behavior, and past settlement outcomes. Despite using zero-shot chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting, PromptLLM attains a 75% agreement rate but only 57.1 final EHI (*100), whereas TACTIC reaches 68.8. Across 20 sequential episodes and three seeds, TACTIC's final EHI improves from 58.2 to 73.2, compared with 65.2 for an ablation without cross-episode updates. Under technology-controls and energy-crisis shocks, TACTIC also exhibits smaller performance degradation than PromptLLM and MemoryLLM. These results indicate that CoT deliberation and interaction memory alone do not fully address delayed execution feedback, whereas settlement-grounded adaptation improves long-horizon negotiation in TradeWar.

title: EvoMCP: Co-evolving MCP agents and training data
body: Supervised fine-tuning of Model Context Protocol (MCP) agents is typically conducted on a static data distribution, which fails to adapt to the student's evolving capabilities and leaves newly exposed weaknesses insufficiently addressed. To address these challenges, we propose \method, an agent--data mutual evolution framework that enables MCP agents to improve through a closed loop of task evolution, trajectory evolution, and supervised fine-tuning. Specifically, \method\ assesses the student's established capabilities and capability gaps from rollout feedback to identify learning targets. Task evolution then translates these targets into executable tasks by adapting the instructions and observable environment states of compatible verified seed tasks while keeping their verifiers aligned. To provide reliable and efficient demonstrations for these tasks, trajectory evolution uses reusable skills to recover failed teacher rollouts and refine successful ones. The resulting task--trajectory pairs are used to fine-tune the student, while accepted tasks seed subsequent evolution. To close the loop, we re-evaluate the updated student and use its feedback to guide the next round of data evolution. Experiments on Toolathlon, MCPMark, and MCP-Atlas demonstrate consistent improvements over the initial student, yielding absolute gains of 16.5\%, 10.2\%, and 12.6\%, respectively. title: Agentic University: Collaborative Agents for Personalized Learning
body: Large language models support personalized tutoring, content generation, and adaptive learning paths. However, capability development requires these resources and interactions to form a coherent learning process that evolves with the learner. A central challenge is to align goals, activities, and assessment while using learning evidence to decide what should follow. We introduce Human-Participatory Multi-Agent Organization and instantiate it in Agentic University (AU). In AU, learners participate as organization members and work with specialized agents to maintain a revisable Capability Program. The program connects personal goals, learning activities across modalities, and layered assessment, while learner feedback and performance guide subsequent support. Our evaluation shows advantages in program organization, assessment design, and revision quality. Users achieved larger mean assessment gains (12.19 versus 5.61 points on a 50-point scale) and reported stronger cognitive support. This work contributes an organizational approach to adaptive learning that makes learner participation a continuing basis for multi-agent coordination. The Agentic University project is available at \href{https://github.com/AgenticOrgLab/AgenticUniversity.git}.

title: Hybrid Computer Use: A Unified Programmatic, Semantic, and Visual Interface for General Agents
body: Computer-use agents increasingly tackle tasks ranging from everyday desktop activities to long-horizon professional workflows. Yet interfaces centered on screenshots and mouse-and-keyboard actions can impose a human-interaction prior, requiring repeated screen interpretation while leaving the computer's semantic and programmatic capabilities underexposed. We argue for exposing these capabilities and letting models choose and combine them. We introduce Hybrid Computer Use (HCU), a unified interface for general agents that combines three complementary channels: programmatic interaction through code and command-line tools, semantic interaction through accessibility (AX), and visual interaction through graphical user interfaces (GUI). Our HCU supports efficient AX interaction and guards against stale-state actions during channel switching. A supplementary HCU skill guides agents in selecting and coordinating channels to use the unified interface effectively. Our designed AX tools return compact observations, execute actions in batches, and report their effects as AX diffs, so the model needs fewer round trips. On OSWorld 2.0, HCU achieves the highest Partial and Binary scores among the compared systems. Analyzing agent trajectories, we find that all evaluated models improve with HCU yet allocate work across the channels differently and consistently outperform compared baselines in terms of both efficiency and task success, highlighting the value of unified computer-use interfaces that allow flexible channel selection and combination.

title: Locating and Closing Information Gaps in Multi-Agent Systems
body: Multi-step Web tasks often require several LLM agents to gather and combine evidence. The communication graph of a fixed workflow restricts which agents can read each other's outputs: evidence retrieved by one agent may never reach the agent that needs it, leaving an information gap and an incomplete or incorrect answer. Adding a connection can deliver the missing evidence, but can also lead the receiver to adopt an incorrect upstream conclusion that displaces a correct answer; the final output alone does not separate the two. We propose Selective Probing and Link Insertion for Closing information gaps in multi-agent Execution (SPLICE), which locates information gaps per query and decides what to adopt after adding an edge. After the original workflow runs, SPLICE uses the query and node outputs to locate a possible gap, adds one directed edge from a source to a receiver to deliver the relevant evidence, and re-executes the receiver and affected downstream nodes, producing a candidate answer. The adoption decision reads both the final answers of the two runs and the process changes the edit caused inside the workflow: how far the receiver moved, where its new content came from, and whether the change reached the final answer. A selector trained on these process features chooses between adopting the candidate answer and retaining the original. On five benchmarks, SPLICE raises the task score on Web tool use by 8.0% and the mean score on four reasoning and planning benchmarks by 5.7% relative to the static skeleton, at 1.25 to 1.44$\times$ the skeleton's cost, and transfers zero-shot to four unseen backbones.

title: Human-in-the-Loop Governance for Agentic AI: Security, Accountability and Decision Control in Enterprise Business Analysis
body: Agentic AI systems plan and act through tools (code execution, database queries, file access, network requests) that enterprises now use for business analysis, and the governance of these systems depends on where a human is kept in the loop. This study asks where human approval gates should sit, how rapidly the software layer through which agents act is being secured, and how accountable its disclosure practice is. The study used every GitHub-reviewed security advisory affecting 365 LLM-application and agent packages on PyPI and npm (N = 2,172 advisories across 346 packages, through 4 October 2026) and mapped each exploit path, using its CWE class, to the control point at which a gate could intercept it. The design is event-historical and Bayesian rather than regression-based: Kaplan–Meier and package-stratified Cox models of vulnerability dwell time and post-disclosure remediation, Bayesian hierarchical models with package random effects for autonomous exploitability, severity and fix-at-disclosure, and a Bayesian decision analysis of gate configurations. Advisory volume rose sharply in 2026 (81.9% of records), led by MCP tool servers and agent frameworks. Agent-action surfaces (prompt injection, execution, queries, file access, network requests and data egress) account for 52.6% of advisories and are more severe but not more autonomously exploitable than platform flaws; the median dwell time of vulnerable code is 248 days and 79.2% of advisories are fixed at disclosure, but the package, rather than the surface, governs remediation speed and most late fixes never arrive. Five approval gates would intercept 59.6% (95% credible interval 55.3–64.0%) of the 499 high- or critical-severity paths that need neither user interaction nor privileges, with execution and egress gates contributing most and returns diminishing quickly. Residual risk, computed as 1 − e × coverage for an assumed, rather than observed, reviewer effectiveness of e, stays above 0.46 at e = 0.9 and cannot fall below 0.40 even with a perfect reviewer, so gates complement rather than replace platform controls. The findings ground a three-tier Human-in-the-Loop Governance Framework (security gates, accountability ledger, decision-control authority) for agentic business analysis.

title: AutoAnalysis: An automated, self-updating meta-analysis of human-AI collaboration
body: As generative artificial intelligence (AI) becomes more capable and widely used, understanding when and how humans should work with these systems is becoming increasingly important. However, the empirical evidence in this space offers conflicting recommendations, which leaves individuals and organizations without clear guidance on when to combine human and AI capabilities. Existing meta-analyses can help reconcile these findings, but they require substantial manual effort and cannot readily incorporate new evidence as it emerges. To address this challenge, we introduce AutoAnalysis: an automated, self-updating meta-analysis of when humans and AI work better together, and when they work better alone. AutoAnalysis' most recent run synthesizes 1,955 effect sizes from 420 papers. Across this body of work, we found that, on average, human-AI combinations performed significantly better than humans alone, but they performed significantly worse than the better of humans or AI alone. These findings highlight the important distinction between improving human performance and achieving human-AI synergy and underscore the need to evaluate collaboration against both human and AI performance alone. As new studies emerge, AutoAnalysis will integrate their findings into the meta-analysis, providing cumulative evidence about when humans and AI perform better together and how human-AI performance varies across AI agents, tasks, and processes.

title: ImplicitHop: Evaluating knowledge integration across context and memory
body: The ability to integrate new information and deduce its consequences is central to learning, understanding, and reasoning in large language models (LLMs). Whether information arrives during training or in-context, models must not only store local facts, but propagate their long-range implications globally. To explore information integration in LLMs, we introduce two complementary natural language benchmarks for large-scale evaluation of deductive reasoning as a function of inference depth. The first is a formal graph benchmark enabling controlled evaluation over a wide range of graph topologies and integration tasks; the second is a knowledge composition benchmark grounded in real-world knowledge graphs. We use these benchmarks to compare knowledge integration from information encoded in context versus information encoded in model weights during pretraining, evaluating a set of open models implicitly, without chain of thought. We find that accuracy decays sharply with increased composition length for both pretrained and in-context knowledge. Information presented in-context, however, substantially outperforms deduction over information encoded in weights. These results quantify a fundamental limitation of current models with direct implications for prompt-based control of agent behavior and for continual learning strategies, and they provide a foundation for developing training, prompting, and integration methods that support deeper reasoning.

title: Counterfactual Pairwise Augmentation Improves Small Pointwise LLM Judges
body: Agentic systems increasingly gate individual steps with a pointwise judge that scores a response against a criterion. Small language models are attractive for this role because they can be served and specialized efficiently. Such a judge must locate the criterion's decision boundary, but pointwise labels under-determine that boundary in fine-tuning: labeled responses to different queries differ along many dimensions at once, so they do not reveal which features decide the label. We introduce CPA (Counterfactual Pairwise Augmentation), which makes the deciding difference explicit in training. For each pointwise item, CPA synthesizes and audits a counterfactual response to the same query intended to carry the opposite label. It frames the accepted pair as a pairwise task asking which of the two responses satisfies the criterion. The judge is fine-tuned jointly on both pointwise and pairwise datasets and deployed in pointwise mode only. A second-order analysis shows when this should outperform the prevailing strategy of merging separately trained pointwise and pairwise experts: merging moves every parameter direction toward the pairwise expert by the same fraction, whereas joint training can hold the pointwise optimum wherever the pairwise loss is flat and absorb its curvature where it is sharp. This is the regime that CPA's same-source, counterfactually minimal pairwise view is designed to produce. On separate Qwen3-8B LoRA adapters for six binary criteria, CPA improves criterion-averaged pointwise macro-F1 by 2.5 points over pointwise-only training and outperforms model merging on all six criteria at every tested merge weight. It also surpasses the strongest zero-shot frontier judge we evaluate, Gemini 3.6 Flash, by 11.8 points.
author: Mohammad Zangooei, Peyvand Teymoori, Mohammad Robati Shirzad, Soroosh Shahtalebi

title: Li$^{2}$SAO: Lifting Light Singl-Rollout Asynchronous RL Optimization via Group-Relative Actor-Critic Bootstrapping
body: Asynchronous reinforcement learning (RL) is becoming a mainstream paradigm for post-training large language models (LLMs), as it improves training efficiency by updating the model as rollouts arrive. Recent work argues that group-wise sampling in GRPO does not naturally fit asynchronous RL training because rollout lengths follow a long-tailed distribution, and proposes Single-rollout Asynchronous Optimization (SAO) to improve stability and off-policy behavior, especially on agentic tasks. However, SAO relies on a closed-source value model obtained from scaling value pretraining. In this paper, we analyze GRPO and LiSAO, our lightweight reproduction of SAO without the pretrained value model, on single-turn reasoning and multi-turn agentic tasks. We find that GRPO outperforms LiSAO on reasoning tasks, while the reverse holds on agentic tasks. Since the value model of LiSAO is not yet well trained , LiSAO lags behind GRPO substantially in early training steps. To address this issue, we propose Li$^{2}$SAO, which Lifts Light Single-rollout Asynchronous Optimization with group-relative actor-critic bootstrapping: while the critic is cold, a group-relative advantage trains the actor and a group-centered return trains the critic, after which training switches to single-rollout GAE. Experiments show that Li$^{2}$SAO catches up with or surpasses GRPO in early training and further raises the later performance ceiling. Code is available at https://github.com/jd-cc-coder/Li2SAO.

title: RoleFUZZER: User-Behaviour Fuzzing for Role-Specification Adherence in Large Language Models
body: Large language models (LLMs) are often conditioned into specific roles such as tutors, interviewers, or agents acting for an organisation, through system prompts that specify how they should behave. The extent to which they can actually adhere to these role specifications under multi-turn interactions with realistic and potentially problematic users is understudied. To address this, we propose user behaviour fuzzing, a guided search over plausible user behaviours that can lead a model to violate its role specification, and introduce RoleFUZZER, a framework that adapts coverage-guided fuzzing from software testing to operationalise the search. RoleFUZZER constructs scenarios guided by a user-behaviour coverage grid that crosses a grounded taxonomy of user interaction types and the role specification of the model under test i.e. what is under pressure. With RoleFUZZER, we evaluate LLMs across five role specifications, including tutor, financial advisor, AI interviewer, antagonistic roleplay character, and web agent under organisational policies. Across simulated and validated conversations in 15 campaigns, the framework reaches >= 89% coverage of the 64-cell behaviour grid for every model and role tested, and surfaces specification-grounded failure patterns. At an equal budget of conversations, removing the RoleFUZZER grid and asking an LLM to generate specification targeting users free-form lowers coverage to 39-69% with fewer kinds of violations. The same specification can also fail in opposite directions. For e.g., on the antagonist, open-weight target models override the player's safety signals, while Claude Haiku 4.5 breaks character instead. RoleFUZZER offers a tractable way to uncover vulnerabilities in LLMs across role specifications by testing diverse user behaviours that are likely to violate them.
